sculpture.reason: A carved wooden totemic figure with painted formline-style face (large ovoid eyes, painted brow shapes) mounted on a shaft, consistent with Northwest Coast/Haida-style carved figures used in ritual or crest contexts.

painting-mss.name: graphics
painting-mss.title: graphics
painting-mss.reason: This is a serigraph print by Haida artist Jim Hart, "Eagle coming out of the Smokehole," made for his Masset totem pole raising at UBC in 1982 — Haida formline art made by a Haida artist, clearly fitting the claimed culture.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photo shows a village scene with carved totem poles, plank houses, and a coastal shoreline, consistent with Haida (or closely related Northwest Coast) architecture and monumental carving—a clear documentary image of traditional dwelling and craft.

photo.name: print
photo.title: print
photo.reason: The image is a printed postcard-style reproduction showing a Haida totem pole and model gabled longhouse, with explanatory text about crest symbolism and house construction — a documentary depiction of genuine Haida material culture (architecture and totem carving).

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph documents a carved argillite Haida bowl with zoomorphic/crest faces carved in relief, a classic Haida art form; this is a documentary photo of an object made by the claimed people.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph documents two carved slate "bear mother" figures (one an original, one a cast), a well-known Haida argillite carving subject, clearly photographed for museum documentation.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph documents a carved wooden rattle in a bear/animal form with characteristic Northwest Coast formline carving, consistent with Haida ceremonial art; it is a documentary studio photo of the object rather than of people, but still depicts something the culture made.

garment.name: Button blanket
garment.title: Button Blanket
garment.reason: This is a classic Haida button blanket with a red-outlined crest figure (bear or frog-like creature) appliquéd in wool trade cloth and outlined with shell buttons, a garment made and worn by Haida and neighboring Northwest Coast peoples for ceremonial regalia.

garment.name: cloak; blanket
garment.title: cloak; blanket
garment.reason: This is a Chilkat-style woven mountain-goat wool ceremonial robe/blanket with a formline face and paired creature design, a classic Northwest Coast garment type made by the Haida, matching the museum's attribution.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: A woven spruce-root basketry hat with formline painted design (eyes, black/red pattern, "slug track" skip stitch), a classic Haida/Northwest Coast form of headwear, well documented as Haida-made.

garment.name: bag; apron; legging
garment.title: bag; apron; legging
garment.reason: A calico and blue Stroud cloth bag with white quillwork design and puffin-beak fringe, part of a medicine man's apron/leggings, attributed by the museum to Haida/Northwest Coast Peoples—consistent with Northwest Coast regalia.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: A woven spruce-root or cedar-bark hat with a tall truncated-cone crown, painted in classic red-and-black Northwest Coast formline design (eyes, curving elements), a well-known Haida woven hat form.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: This is a woven spruce-root conical hat painted with formline designs (faces, ovoid eyes, black-red-black palette), a classic Northwest Coast style closely associated with Haida and neighboring peoples' traditional dress and ceremonial regalia.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: This is a spruce-root basketry hat painted with formline-style crest imagery, a well-documented Haida/Northwest Coast tradition; the woven form and painted design are consistent with Haida-made dress items.

garment.name: bag; apron; legging
garment.title: bag; apron; legging
garment.reason: This is a quillwork-decorated apron/bag element with puffin-beak fringe, a form and technique associated with Northwest Coast Indigenous regalia (medicine man's dance apron), consistent with a Haida-attributed garment component even though this style of quillwork and puffin-beak ornamentation is common across several Northwest Coast peoples.

ceramic.name: bowl
ceramic.title: bowl
ceramic.reason: This is a classic Haida argillite carving, a bowl in the form of a crouching bear with abalone shell inlaid eyes and bone inlay teeth — argillite carving is a distinctive Haida art tradition, and the museum confirms Haida attribution.

ceramic.name: dish
ceramic.title: dish
ceramic.reason: This is a finely carved argillite dish with incised spiral and cross-hatch designs and inlaid ivory/shell insets — argillite carving is a distinctive Haida art form, and this type of engraved, inlaid dish matches known Haida trade-ware production.

ceramic.name: bowl
ceramic.title: bowl
ceramic.reason: An argillite bowl carved in beaver/bird effigy form, a well-documented Haida art form using stone quarried on Haida Gwaii, and the museum directly attributes it to Haida makers.

ceramic.name: bowl
ceramic.title: bowl
ceramic.reason: This is a black argillite bowl carved with totemic imagery (apparently a bear/animal form), a distinctive Haida craft material and style from the Queen Charlotte Islands, consistent with the claimed ethnicity and provenance noted on the museum label.

architectural.name: door-frame
architectural.title: door-frame
architectural.reason: The image shows a carved wooden totemic doorway/houseposts with crest figures (owl-like eagle/thunderbird and raven) and an entrance cut at the base, a classic Northwest Coast Haida architectural feature.

architectural.name: photographic print
architectural.title: photographic print (black and white)
architectural.reason: The image shows a carved Haida totem pole with multiple crest figures standing before the timber frame of a traditional house at Kayang, a documented Haida village site—clear evidence of Haida monumental carving and architecture.

architectural.name: print
architectural.title: print
architectural.reason: The image shows a print/photograph of a carved Haida-style totem pole standing before a wooden gabled longhouse model, both traditional Haida architectural and sculptural forms. This is documentary depiction of genuine Haida material culture, fitting the claimed ethnicity.

architectural.name: photographic print
architectural.title: photographic print (black and white)
architectural.reason: The photograph shows a monumental wooden Haida tomb structure (a mortuary post/gateway with painted crest panel) at Masset, a documented Haida village, consistent with Haida mortuary architecture traditions.

textile.name: mat
textile.title: mat
textile.reason: The image shows a woven cedar bark mat with a plaid-like pattern, a traditional Northwest Coast craft form consistent with Haida material culture.

metalwork.name: copper
metalwork.title: copper
metalwork.reason: This is a classic Northwest Coast ceremonial copper shield, with the T-ridge form and painted/engraved crest face design (formline eyes and mouth) typical of Haida and neighboring groups' prestige objects. It fits the claimed metalwork category and Haida attribution.

metalwork.name: crooked knife
metalwork.title: crooked knife
metalwork.reason: This is a crooked knife with a curved bone/antler handle and steel blade, a classic Northwest Coast carving tool used by Haida and neighbouring peoples for woodworking; the object type fits the claimed ethnicity even though the metal blade is a minor secondary component to the bone handle.
